tips.title: The limit is in the ear
tips.body: Air carries a 30 kHz sound perfectly well — a bat hears it. What stops **you** is that your ear drum does not convert that frequency into a useful vibration. The restriction is on the **conversion**, not on the wave.

tips.title: 20 kHz is 20 000 Hz
tips.body: Substituting 20 instead of 20 000 into $\lambda = v/f$ gives 17 m instead of 1.7 cm — a thousand times too big, and at the wrong end of the range. Convert the prefix before you divide.

tips.title: One example of each direction
tips.body: A question on converting **between** sound and vibration wants both ways: **ear drum** or microphone one way, **loudspeaker cone** or tuning fork the other. Three examples of the same direction answer half the question.

tips.title: Closer particles mean faster sound
tips.body: Counter-intuitive, so give the reason. Sound is a **disturbance passed particle to particle**, not an object moving through the material — so close, strongly bonded particles pass it on **sooner**.

tips.title: Physics only, Higher tier only
tips.body: Spec point 4.6.1.4 is not on combined science and not on the Foundation paper. Worth knowing before you spend revision time on it.

why.matters:
A sound wave is nothing but air being squashed and stretched. It becomes a **sound** only when something solid is made to vibrate by it — and in your case that solid is an ear drum.

Putting it that way answers the question the topic is really about. Your hearing stops at 20 kHz not because the air gives up, but because **that conversion** does. A bat hears 30 kHz in the same air you are standing in. The limit is in you. The same swap runs the other way in every loudspeaker and every instrument ever built.

examples.title: Why an unplugged electric guitar is so quiet
examples.body:
A vibrating string barely makes a sound. It is 65 cm long and about a millimetre thick, so it has roughly 6.5 cm² of surface to push air with, and it slices through the air rather than shifting it.

An acoustic guitar fixes that. The string drives the bridge, the bridge drives the wooden top, and the top is about 1 320 cm² — some **200 times** more air moved by the same vibration. A solid-body electric has no such top, which is why you can practise on one next to someone watching television.

props.caption: The same vibration, given two hundred times the area to work with.

visual.alt: Two bars to scale showing a guitar's wooden top at about thirteen hundred square centimetres against the six and a half square centimetres of the string that drives it

examples.title: Why your own voice sounds wrong on a recording
examples.body:
Everyone else hears your voice one way: out of your mouth, through the air, into their ear drum. You hear it twice. The air path, and a second one straight through the bone of your skull to the inner ear — a solid carrying the vibration, which is this topic's own sentence in action.

Bone carries the low frequencies better than air does, so the voice in your head has a bass lift nobody else gets. A recording keeps only the air path. The thin, higher stranger on the playback is what you actually sound like.

examples.title: Under water you cannot tell where a sound came from
examples.body:
Your ears are about 18 cm apart, and most of how you place a sound is the tiny gap between one ear hearing it and the other. In air the biggest that gap can be is 0.53 of a millisecond.

Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water rather than 340, so under water the same head gives at most 0.12 ms — 4.4 times smaller, and below what the brain can use. Divers report a sound as simply everywhere at once. Faster sound is the topic's own rule, and this is the price of it.

props.title: Your ears are 18 cm apart, and that gap is all you get

steps.title: Where this sits
steps.body:
**This topic is physics only and Higher tier only.** It is not on the combined science course, and it is not on the Foundation paper. If you are taking separate Physics at Higher tier, it is examinable; otherwise it is useful background for the waves you do study.

You already know that **sound is a longitudinal wave**: the air vibrates back and forth **along** the direction the sound travels, making **compressions** where particles are pushed together and **rarefactions** where they spread apart.

What this topic adds is what happens when sound meets something that is **not** air — a solid — and what that has to do with **hearing**.

boxes.title: Why it matters
points: it explains how the ear works

steps.title: Sound in solids
steps.body:
**Sound waves can travel through solids, causing vibrations in the solid.**

This works both ways, and that two-way conversion is the heart of the topic:

- a **sound wave in air** can make a **solid vibrate**
- a **vibrating solid** can make a **sound wave in air**

A loudspeaker does the second: an electrical signal makes a cone vibrate, and the vibrating cone pushes on the air. A microphone does the first: sound in the air makes a diaphragm vibrate, and that vibration is turned into a signal.

**Sound travels faster in solids than in liquids, and faster in liquids than in gases.** The reason is the spacing of the particles. In a solid the particles are close together and strongly bonded, so a push on one is passed to the next almost immediately. In a gas the particles are far apart, so the disturbance takes longer to pass along.

That is why you can hear a train coming by putting your ear to the rail before you hear it through the air — the sound reaches you through the steel first.

**The general rule:** closer particles mean faster sound.

steps.title: How the ear works
steps.body:
**Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, which causes the sensation of sound.**

That is the spec's own sentence, and it is worth learning close to word for word, because every part of it earns something.

**The chain:**

1. A **sound wave in air** arrives at the ear.
2. It makes the **ear drum vibrate** — a sound wave converted into a vibration of a solid.
3. The ear drum passes the vibration to **other parts** inside the ear, which also vibrate.
4. Those vibrations produce the **sensation of sound**.

**The ear drum is a solid being made to vibrate by a sound wave** — exactly the process described in the last step. The ear is not a special case; it is the same physics as a microphone diaphragm.

**And here is the point the whole topic turns on.** That conversion — sound wave to vibration of a solid — **only works over a limited frequency range**. The ear drum and the parts behind it have a size and a stiffness, and they respond well only to vibrations within a certain band. Outside it, the sound arrives but the solid does not vibrate usefully, so no sensation of sound is produced.

**This restricts the limits of human hearing.** Our hearing range is not set by the air or by the sound; it is set by **what our ear drum can respond to**.

steps.title: The range of human hearing
steps.body:
**You are expected to know this range:**

$$\textbf{20 Hz to 20 000 Hz} \qquad \text{that is, 20 Hz to 20 kHz}$$

**20 kHz means 20 kilohertz, which is 20 000 Hz.** Getting the prefix wrong by a factor of a thousand is an easy mark to lose.

**What those limits look like as wavelengths.** Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s and using $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$:

- at **20 Hz**: $\lambda = \dfrac{340}{20} = 17$ m — longer than a house
- at **20 000 Hz**: $\lambda = \dfrac{340}{20\,000} = 0.017$ m — about 1.7 cm

So across the audible range the wavelength changes by a factor of **a thousand**, from seventeen metres down to under two centimetres. The frequency range spans the same factor, which it must, because at a fixed speed the two are inversely proportional.

**Two words worth having:**

- **Infrasound** — below 20 Hz, too low to hear.
- **Ultrasound** — above 20 kHz, too high to hear. This is the same ultrasound used for medical imaging, and it connects directly to the *Waves for detection and exploration* topic.

**The range narrows with age**, mostly at the top end. That is why a device emitting a tone at around 17 kHz can be audible to teenagers and inaudible to adults — the physics has not changed, but the ear has.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The limit is in the ear, not in the sound.** This is the single idea the topic is built on, and it is the one most often got backwards. Air carries a 30 kHz sound perfectly well; a bat hears it without difficulty. What stops *you* hearing it is that **your ear drum and the parts behind it do not convert that frequency into a useful vibration**. The spec's wording is careful: *the conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range. This restricts the limits of human hearing.* The restriction is on the **conversion**, not on the wave.

**Say which conversion, in which direction.** A question asking for examples of processes converting between sound waves and vibrations of solids wants both directions:

- **sound to vibration**: the ear drum, a microphone diaphragm, a window rattling in a gale
- **vibration to sound**: a loudspeaker cone, a guitar string driving the body of the instrument, a tuning fork

Naming one of each is worth more than naming three of the same kind.

**Faster in solids is counter-intuitive, so give the reason.** People expect a dense solid to slow a wave down, as it would slow a moving object. Sound is not an object travelling through the material — it is a **disturbance passed from particle to particle**. Closer, more strongly bonded particles pass it on **sooner**, so the wave goes faster.

**Watch the kilo.** 20 kHz is **20 000 Hz**. Substituting 20 into $\lambda = v/f$ gives 17 m instead of 1.7 cm — an answer a thousand times too big, at the wrong end of the range.

**Connect it to ultrasound.** Above 20 kHz is ultrasound, which is exactly what medical imaging and echo sounding use. The reason those applications use it is partly this topic: a higher frequency means a **shorter wavelength**, and a shorter wavelength can resolve smaller detail. So the upper limit of hearing is also, usefully, the lower limit of a whole technology.

**And ageing.** Hearing narrows with age, mostly at the top. It is a change in the ear, not in physics — which is the same point as the first one, arriving from a different direction.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- This spec point is **physics only** and **Higher tier only**.
- **Sound is longitudinal**: compressions and rarefactions along the direction of travel.
- **Sound waves can travel through solids, causing vibrations in the solid.**
- The conversion works **both ways**: sound makes solids vibrate, and vibrating solids make sound.
- Examples: **ear drum** and **microphone diaphragm** one way; **loudspeaker cone** and **guitar string** the other.
- Sound travels **fastest in solids**, then liquids, then gases, because **closer particles pass the disturbance on sooner**.
- In the ear, sound waves cause the **ear drum and other parts to vibrate**, which causes the **sensation of sound**.
- That conversion works only over a **limited frequency range**, and this **restricts the limits of human hearing**.
- **The limit is in the ear, not in the sound or the air.**
- Normal human hearing runs from **20 Hz to 20 kHz**, that is **20 000 Hz**.
- At 340 m/s those correspond to wavelengths of **17 m** and **0.017 m**.
- Below 20 Hz is **infrasound**; above 20 kHz is **ultrasound**.
- Hearing narrows with **age**, mostly at the top end.

questions.prompt: Explain how the ear detects sound, and explain why human hearing has an upper and a lower limit.
questions.solution: A sound wave travelling through the air is a longitudinal wave, consisting of compressions where the air particles are pushed close together and rarefactions where they are spread further apart. When this wave reaches the ear it arrives at the ear drum, which is a thin solid membrane, and the varying pressure of the wave causes the ear drum to vibrate. This is an example of a sound wave being converted into a vibration of a solid. The ear drum then passes the vibration on to other parts within the ear, which also vibrate, and these vibrations ultimately cause the sensation of sound. Human hearing has limits because this conversion of sound waves into vibrations of solids only works over a limited range of frequencies. The ear drum and the structures behind it have a particular size and stiffness, and they respond well only to vibrations within a certain band. Outside that band the sound wave still arrives at the ear, and the air carries it perfectly well, but it is not converted into a useful vibration and so no sensation of sound is produced. It is important to be clear that the limitation lies in the ear and not in the sound or in the air. The normal range of human hearing runs from twenty hertz up to twenty kilohertz, which is twenty thousand hertz. Sound below this range is called infrasound and sound above it is called ultrasound, and a bat can hear frequencies well above our upper limit. The upper limit also falls with age.

questions.modelAnswer:
**How the ear detects sound:**

1. A **longitudinal** sound wave — compressions and rarefactions — travels through the air to the ear.
2. Its varying pressure makes the **ear drum vibrate**. This is a **sound wave converted into a vibration of a solid**.
3. The ear drum passes the vibration to **other parts** of the ear, which also vibrate.
4. Those vibrations cause the **sensation of sound**.

**Why there are limits.** That conversion works only over a **limited frequency range**. The ear drum and the structures behind it have a size and a stiffness, and respond well only within a certain band.

**The mark most often missed:** outside the band, the sound **still arrives** and the air carries it perfectly well — it simply is not converted. **The limit is in the ear, not in the sound.**

**The range** is **20 Hz to 20 kHz** (20 000 Hz). Below is **infrasound**, above is **ultrasound** — and a bat hears well above our limit, which is the clearest proof that the restriction is ours.

questions.prompt: Describe, with examples, processes that convert between sound waves and vibrations in solids, and explain why sound travels faster in a solid than in a gas.
questions.solution: Sound waves and vibrations in solids can be converted into one another in both directions, and a full answer should give an example of each. In the first direction, a sound wave travelling through the air causes a solid to vibrate. The clearest example is the ear drum, a thin membrane which is set vibrating by the varying pressure of an arriving sound wave, and a microphone works on the same principle, with a diaphragm that vibrates in response to the sound reaching it. A window rattling as a heavy lorry passes is the same process on a larger scale. In the second direction, a vibrating solid produces a sound wave in the surrounding air. A loudspeaker cone is driven back and forth by an electrical signal and pushes on the air, creating compressions and rarefactions, and a struck tuning fork or the body of a guitar driven by its strings does the same thing. Sound travels faster in a solid than in a gas because of the spacing and bonding of the particles. Sound is not an object moving through a material but a disturbance passed from one particle to the next. In a solid the particles are close together and strongly bonded, so when one particle is displaced it pushes on its neighbour almost immediately and the disturbance is passed on very quickly. In a gas the particles are far apart and must travel some distance before colliding with the next, so the disturbance takes longer to pass along and the wave travels more slowly. This is why the sound of an approaching train can be heard through the rail before it is heard through the air.

**Both directions, and a full answer gives one of each:**

- **Sound to vibration**: an **ear drum** set vibrating by an arriving wave; a **microphone diaphragm**; a **window rattling** as a lorry passes.
- **Vibration to sound**: a **loudspeaker cone** pushing on the air; a struck **tuning fork**; a **guitar body** driven by its strings.

Naming three examples of the same direction answers only half the question.

**Why sound is faster in a solid.** Sound is **not an object moving through** the material — it is a **disturbance passed from particle to particle**.

- In a **solid** the particles are **close and strongly bonded**, so a displaced particle pushes its neighbour almost immediately.
- In a **gas** the particles are **far apart** and must travel before colliding, so the disturbance takes longer to pass along.

**The everyday evidence:** an approaching train can be heard through the **rail** before it is heard through the **air**.

This is worth stating carefully because it is counter-intuitive — people expect a dense solid to slow a wave down, as it would slow a moving object.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer puts the limit where it belongs: in the ear. It knows the air carries ultrasound perfectly well and that a bat hears it, so the restriction is on the conversion of sound into vibration and not on the wave. It gives one example of each direction of conversion without being prompted twice, explains the speed in solids by how the disturbance is passed between particles rather than by density, and converts 20 kHz to 20 000 Hz before it calculates anything. It also sees that the upper limit of hearing is the lower limit of ultrasound, and therefore of medical imaging and echo sounding.
